item.title: Neighbors sue Marin County over housing project at Strawberry seminary site
item.description: The suit argues the county improperly waived the Strawberry Community Plan's ban on housing atop Chapel Hill, and that its environmental review fell short.
item.content:encoded:
A Strawberry neighbors’ group is suing Marin County to overturn its approval of a project that would remake the former Golden Gate Baptist Theological Seminary site into hundreds of homes, a senior-care facility and a graduate school.

Strawberry Residents for Sensible Development filed suit July 6 in Marin Superior Court. North Coast Land Holdings, the project’s developer, is named in the case as a real party in interest, meaning it can also defend the project in court. The litigation could delay a project that has drawn public debate for more than a decade.

On June 9, the Board of Supervisors voted unanimously to approve North Coast’s plan for the hilltop site. The hearing drew about two dozen public speakers, most of them critical.

North Coast has worked through years of negotiations since buying the site in 2014, including a March 1 settlement with the Seminary Neighborhood Association, which agreed to drop its opposition to the project. But other Strawberry residents say the association represents only a small group and doesn’t speak for those who still object to the project.

The new resident group is part of that continued opposition. Its founder said a July 28 community meeting drew at least 30 residents. The group contends the approved project violates the Strawberry Community Plan and state environmental law.

The lawsuit makes two broad legal claims, both centered on Chapel Hill. North Coast plans 40 market-rate homes there, a mix of one- to four-bedroom units.

First, the lawsuit argues the county improperly waived the Strawberry Community Plan’s ban on housing atop Chapel Hill under state density-bonus law. The county’s own environmental review had found that an alternative design, which would meet the same density without the waiver, was environmentally superior. The lawsuit says the Board of Supervisors rejected that alternative without giving any reasoning.

Second, the lawsuit argues the environmental review required under the California Environmental Quality Act fell short. It says the review did not adequately assess the visual impact of developing Chapel Hill, including the loss of bay views; the raising of the athletic field with 220,000 cubic yards of excavated soil; the displacement of low-income residents whose homes would be demolished; or the county’s reliance on a 1953 permit that allowed up to 1,000 students on the site.

Attorney Michael Graf represents the group. The lawsuit...
item.dc:creator: Tyler Callister
item.media:description: A site plan for the former Golden Gate Baptist Theological Seminary shows homes planned for the Chapel Hill area, at center right, ringing an open square at the hilltop rather than covering it. A neighbors' lawsuit says the Strawberry Community Plan bars housing atop Chapel Hill; the county says the buildings would sit on the slopes. (Mark Cavagnero Associates Architects via Marin County)

item.title: Underwater robot to chart Richardson Bay's eelgrass meadows
item.description: So far the project only maps and monitors. The agency hopes to fund robotic planting next, with a $1.9 million grant.
item.content:encoded:
Like the shark it’s named for, Mako will cruise silently along the floor of Richardson Bay, hunting. But this predator is a robot, and what it’s hunting is eelgrass — the waving undersea meadows that are vital to the bay’s ecology.

Starting this month, the Richardson Bay Regional Agency will use an underwater drone to map and monitor Richardson Bay eelgrass beds. The bay agency has enlisted San Francisco-based Ulysses Ecosystem Engineering to study eelgrass beds using an autonomous underwater vehicle named Mako.

A $250,000 grant from the Marin Community Foundation will fund the project, a one-year award running through June 30, 2027.

Eelgrass is an ecological scaffold for marine life, home to a host of invertebrates and a preferred spawning ground for herring. Studies have shown it buffers wave action, improves water quality and sequesters carbon dioxide from the atmosphere. Richardson Bay’s eelgrass beds are the second largest in San Francisco Bay and among the largest on the West Coast. Eelgrass, however, is in retreat worldwide because of shoreline development and pollution.
item.dc:creator: Gretchen Lang
item.media:description: Mako, Ulysses Ecosystem Engineering’s autonomous underwater drone, passes over a seagrass meadow off Perth, Australia. The Richardson Bay Regional Agency will use the drone starting this month to map and monitor eelgrass beds in the bay. (via Ulysses)

item.title: Tiburon promotes officer as Police Department adds fifth sergeant
item.description: Tiburon has added a fifth police sergeant and cut an officer position, promoting Justin Hettich, who had covered supervisor shifts since January 2025.
item.content:encoded:
Tiburon has added a fifth police sergeant position and reduced its authorized patrol officers by one, promoting an officer who had covered supervisor shifts since January 2025.

Justin Hettich’s promotion took effect July 1. The department announced it in a July 27 Instagram post, saying he has worked in law enforcement for more than 18 years, six of them in Tiburon.

The promotion leaves the department with five sergeants and six officers, along with four reserve officers, Police Chief Michelle Jean said. One of the six, Officer William Forrest Condit, has been on paid administrative leave since October, leaving five officers available for patrol. One of the five sergeants, Rob Law, works full time as a detective.

The supervisory opening dates to January 2025, when Law moved to detective duties under a six-month pilot program. Jean said that shift left a patrol team without a supervising sergeant and that Hettich has served as officer in charge since that month.
item.dc:creator: Tyler Callister
item.media:description: Justin Hettich was promoted to Tiburon police sergeant effective July 1, filling a fifth sergeant position the town added in its new budget. Hettich joined the department in 2020 and had covered supervisor shifts as officer in charge since January 2025. (via Tiburon Police Department)

item.title: Consultant says proposed wall would worsen flooding in Tiburon's Bel Aire neighborhood
item.description: A consultant is advising against a proposed flood wall on one of the creeks that floods Tiburon's Bel Aire neighborhood, saying it would push water onto homes that don't flood now.
item.content:encoded:
The consultant designing a restoration project for two creeks that flood Tiburon’s Bel Aire neighborhood in heavy rain is advising against a proposed flood wall on one of them. The wall would push flooding into parts of the neighborhood that don’t flood now, the firm’s modeling found.

Officials delivered that update and detailed how work will proceed on the East and West creeks project during the July 28 Marin Flood Control District Zone 4 advisory board meeting, which featured only informational items and no votes.

The board also heard updates on a planned study addressing chronic flooding near Greenwood Cove Drive and a potential study evaluating levees near Strawberry Circle following tidal flooding in January.

The zone covers Tiburon’s Bel Aire neighborhood, parts of unincorporated Tiburon along Greenwood Cove Drive and homes along Strawberry Circle.
item.dc:creator: Francisco Martinez
item.media:description: Verdantas hydrologist Janice Weldon showcases inundation modeling along the lower West Creek during a 50-year storm, or a storm with a 2% chance of occurring in a given year, during the Marin Flood Control District Zone 4 advisory board meeting July 28 at Westminster Presbyterian Church. The inundation projection does not account for pumping from the Cecilia Way and Cove pump stations. (Francisco Martinez / The Ark)

item.title: Socal man sues Tiburon, Marin, PG&E over trip-and-fall
item.description: An Orange County man is suing Tiburon, Marin County and PG&E, saying a steel utility vault cover in the downtown sidewalk shifted under his weight and dropped him to the pavement.
item.content:encoded:
A Southern California man says a steel utility-vault cover embedded in the sidewalk in downtown Tiburon shifted under his weight and dropped him to the pavement, and he is suing the town, Marin County and Pacific Gas and Electric Co. over the injuries.

Daniel Byun, 55, of Orange County filed the complaint July 10 in Marin County Superior Court. It alleges the town and county created “an unreasonably dangerous condition” by failing to maintain the sidewalk near Fountain Plaza downtown, and that PG&E, as owner of the vault and its cover, failed to inspect and maintain the cover.

Byun first filed a claim against the town and county on or about Dec. 15, 2025, the complaint says. The county and town each rejected it the next month, clearing the way for the suit.

The complaint does not name a dollar figure. It says only that the damages exceed $35,000, the minimum for an unlimited civil case, and asks a jury to set the amount at trial.

Saul Wolf, one of Byun’s attorneys at Costa Mesa-based Easton & Easton LLP, told The Ark in a July 29 interview that the fall left Byun with fractured ribs, shoulder sprains, a torn biceps, a damaged knee and neck and back pain.
item.dc:creator: Francisco Martinez

item.title: DA declines to charge Tiburon man in alleged kidnapping of girlfriend
item.description: The Marin County District Attorney's Office has declined to file charges against an 18-year-old Tiburon man arrested in June on suspicion of kidnapping and robbing his girlfriend.
item.content:encoded:
The Marin County District Attorney’s Office has declined to file criminal charges against an 18-year-old Tiburon man who was arrested in June on suspicion of kidnapping and robbing his 17-year-old girlfriend.

The man surrendered at the Tiburon police station with his attorney June 16 and was booked into Marin County Jail on suspicion of kidnapping, robbery, child cruelty and false imprisonment. He was released the same day. Because prosecutors filed no charges, The Ark is not naming him under a policy of generally not identifying suspects before they are formally charged.

Police said the case stemmed from an argument shortly after 2 a.m. June 15, while the couple sat in a parked car near Heathcliff Drive. The man then began driving, and the girl tried to get out, but he put the car in reverse and accelerated with her door still open, police said. She tried to call 911, and he took her phone. The car stopped on Avenida Miraflores, near Del Mar Middle School, where she got out.

The girl ran to a nearby home and knocked, but no one answered, police said. She then walked alone to the police station to report what happened.

In the meantime, the man had gone to her father’s home in Mill Valley to say the girl had fled the car, police said. He returned her phone to the father, and the two men drove back toward Avenida Miraflores to look for her. Her father called police to report her missing, and officers were treating it as a missing-juvenile case when they arrived.

Police said the allegations of force and restraint came from the girl’s account to officers at the station.

A cite hearing, or pre-arraignment appearance, had been scheduled for July 28. The district attorney’s office confirmed July 30 that it did not file a criminal complaint.
item.dc:creator: Kevin Hessel

item.title: Third owner wins Belvedere's approval for hillside home project
item.description: It's the same design the commission approved nine years ago. The architect called it "the exact design that was approved in June of 2017," apart from an outdoor inclined lift.
item.content:encoded:
Three owners have won Belvedere’s approval to build a mansion at 135 Belvedere Ave. since 2017. The first two sold the lot instead, the second at a $1.7 million loss, leaving a derelict 1957 house and a hillside of collapsing Monterey pines.

On July 21, the Planning Commission approved the third try — an 11,223-square-foot contemporary home more than twice the size zoning allows, and the same design it approved nine years ago.

The commission voted 4-0 to grant design review, a demolition permit and an exception to the city’s floor-area cap for architect David Kotzebue’s design, and to recommend City Council approval of a revocable license for private improvements in the city’s right of way.

The new home would replace a 3,764-square-foot residence on a steeply sloped, 52,965-square-foot lot overlooking Richardson Bay.

item.media:description: A rendering shows the 11,223-square-foot home approved for 135 Belvedere Ave. The Belvedere Planning Commission voted 4-0 July 21 to approve architect David Kotzebue’s design, granting an exception that allows more than twice the floor area zoning permits on the site. (David Kotzebue Architecture via city of Belvedere)

item.title: New Business: Club Pilates adds to fitness scene at Strawberry Village
item.description: Club Pilates has opened at Strawberry Village, joining a cluster of fitness businesses that already includes Pure Barre, Orangetheory, StretchLab and Hot Yoga Republic.
item.content:encoded:
Club Pilates opened June 25 in the Strawberry Village shopping center. The studio sits between Hot Yoga Republic and the recently opened Hydration Room. Club Pilates is the world’s largest Pilates brand, with more than 1,400 studios worldwide. The company operates more than 1,000 studios in North America and has expanded to 12 countries. Other Marin locations include Greenbrae, Novato and San Rafael.

Club Pilates offers classes seven days a week, focused on the Pilates “reformer,” a bed-like frame with a sliding carriage, adjustable springs for resistance, ropes, pulleys and a foot bar. The method was created by Joseph Pilates, a German-born fitness pioneer who overcame childhood illnesses by taking up gymnastics, boxing and yoga. The method emphasizes mindful breathing, precise movement and control.

“It’s not just about flexibility, which is kind of the misconception,” general manager Emma Roberts says. “You don’t have to be flexible to take Pilates. It can help you with your flexibility, but overall, it’s a low-impact form of exercise that just helps you continue to be active without hurting yourself.”
item.dc:creator: Tyler Callister
item.media:description: General manager Emma Roberts sits on a reformer at Club Pilates, which opened June 25 at the Strawberry Village shopping center. The studio, part of a chain with more than 1,400 locations, offers classes seven days a week built around the machine’s sliding carriage and spring resistance. (Tyler Callister / The Ark)

item.title: Everyday Encounters: A tech career gives way to quieter days
item.description: Crystal Thomas has a chair outside the Belvedere-Tiburon Library, an umbrella for shade and nowhere she needs to be. She is a year into a break from a career in tech.
item.content:encoded:
Crystal Thomas has a chair outside the Belvedere-Tiburon Library, an umbrella for shade and nowhere she needs to be.

She’s reading “The Assassin’s Blade,” a collection of prequel novellas in author Sarah J. Maas’ “Throne of Glass” fantasy series. Thomas, who has lived in Tiburon for four years, started reading fantasy only earlier this year but already counts herself a fan.

“It’s a little slow to get into because it’s world-building,” Thomas, 47, says July 29. “All the character building and the environment … it’s kind of like ‘Game of Thrones,’ you know — it takes a while to get into.”

She has the time. Thomas is a year into a break from a career in technology, most recently at Google, where she worked in cloud computing and artificial-intelligence infrastructure. She has also worked at Apple and IBM, among other companies.
item.dc:creator: Francisco Martinez
item.media:description: Tiburon resident Crystal Thomas says she’s enjoying time away from work after 27 years of a ‘schedule that’s hour-by-hour.’ Thomas was reading ‘The Assassin’s Blade’ outside the Belvedere-Tiburon Library on July 29. (Francisco Martinez / The Ark)

item.title: Candidate filings accelerate ahead of Friday’s first deadline
item.description: Thirteen candidates filed for peninsula races between July 27 and Aug. 3. Filing closes Aug. 7 in most races, with extensions where an incumbent bows out.
item.content:encoded:
Four candidates have now qualified for the Nov. 3 ballot in Tiburon — among them two challengers — ensuring a contested race for three Town Council seats. Mayor Jon Welner has taken out nomination papers to seek a third term but had not filed by press time.

The moves came during a rush of activity across races on peninsula ballots. Thirteen candidates filed between July 27 and Aug. 3, and five other residents took out nomination papers. The filings included two incumbents whose plans had been unclear, and challengers emerged in two races that had drawn none.

Welner, the last of the three Tiburon incumbents to act, took out papers July 28. Incumbents Alice Fredericks and Jack Ryan filed July 29 and qualified the same day. Fredericks, first elected in 2001, is seeking a seventh term.

Chuck Hornbrook, who serves on the town’s Parks, Open Space & Trails Commission, became the first challenger to file, turning in his papers July 30 and qualifying July 31. Wealth-management firm founder Faris Jafar filed and qualified Aug. 3.

Welner has until 5 p.m. Aug. 7. If he doesn’t file, other challengers would have until 5 p.m. 12 to enter the race.

In Belvedere, there was no new activity. Both incumbents remain qualified and unopposed for two seats. Councilmember Peter Mark qualified July 16, and Councilmember Jane Cooper qualified July 23. Both were first elected in 2022 and seek second terms, their last under a local custom that limits members to two terms. With both incumbents in, filing closes Aug. 7.

Interested residents may obtain Tiburon council nomination papers from Town Clerk Lea Dilena at 415-435-7377 orldilena@townoftiburon.govand Belvedere council papers from City Clerk Beth Haener at 415-435-8913 orclerk@cityofbelvedere.org.

Other races on the ballot

Reed Union School District:Four candidates have now filed for the three seats. Challengers Lina Godfrey, a Tiburon resident and disability-access advocate who serves on the town’s Diversity Inclusion Task Force, and Krupa Antani, a Tiburon resident and Reed Union parent volunteer, filed July 27 and July 28, respectively. They join incumbents Mike Ghaffary, who filed July 14, and board President Shelby Pasarell Tsai, who filed July 22. Board member Afsaneh Zolfaghari is not seeking reelection, and because she is not expected to file, challengers would have until Aug. 12 to enter the race.

item.title: Belvedere says MCE board needs broad overhaul, not just expertise
item.description: Mayor Sally Wilkinson, Belvedere's MCE representative, wants the 34-member board replaced. "The real question is whether the current board is willing to sack itself."
item.content:encoded:
By TYLER CALLISTER and KEVIN HESSEL

Belvedere has told the Marin civil grand jury it agrees the board governing the region’s public electricity provider is short on expertise and that its members often fail to show up, but it balked at the jury’s prescription for fixing the problem.

The June 16 report found that the board of MCE, the four-county agency once known as Marin Clean Energy that supplies the electricity for most Belvedere residents, had “rarely asserted its responsibility of governance,” while management “appeared to be taking advantage of this situation.” Jurors started digging after the agency’s power costs jumped nearly $200 million in a single year. The day after the report came out, MCE’s longtime chief executive, Dawn Weisz, was gone.

The City Council approved Belvedere’s response unanimously without discussion July 13, agreeing with both findings the jury directed at member cities: that board members have limited expertise for an agency as complex as MCE, and that poor attendance has undercut its oversight. It also agreed with one of the two required recommendations, that cities commit their appointees to attending every board meeting.

Belvedere objected to the second recommendation, the jury’s remedy for the expertise problem: a call for cities to reassess their appointments and pick the members with the most financial and energy expertise. Not every council has such a member, Belvedere wrote, and the recommendation is “at best, an interim measure” that does nothing about the size and structure of a 34-member board.

Mayor Sally Wilkinson, the city’s representative on the MCE board since December 2020, brought the response to the council in a staff report with City Manager Robert Zadnik. Her part in it does not end with Belvedere’s letter. The MCE board on July 16 appointed her to the ad hoc committee of Marin and Contra Costa County officials that will draft the agency’s own reply. Working with staff and a governance attorney, the committee is to bring it to the full board to consider Aug. 20.
item.dc:creator: Tyler Callister

item.title: Tiburon resident wins fair contest with iPhone shot
item.description: It was Jennifer Isaac's first time entering the county fair. She says she was "shocked, excited, elated, jumping up and down" when she heard.
item.content:encoded:
Jennifer Isaac had already finished her docent-led tour of the Marin County Civic Center when she turned back for one last look — and stopped.

“(I) was just struck by the shapes all over again,” the Tiburon resident says of the building, designed by architect Frank Lloyd Wright.

She pulled out her iPhone, framed the arches from above and captured what she saw. A little routine editing later — converting to black and white, intensifying the contrast, cropping — and she had a photo. What she didn’t know was that she also had the top prize at the Marin County Fair.

The 71-year-old won for her picture, “Marin Civic Center Aspect,” in the cityscapes and architecture class for monochromatic fine photography at the fair, held July 1-5.
item.dc:creator: Francisco Martinez
item.media:description: In her photo ‘Marin Civic Center Aspect,’ Jennifer Isaac says she looked to capture the building in a way that would offer ‘something a bit different to say about the Civic Center,’ focusing on its arches from above. (Jennifer Isaac)

item.title: Belvedere’s ‘Toy Story 5’ director reflects on career and what’s ahead
item.description: Belvedere's Andrew Stanton directed "Toy Story 5," which has grossed more than $900 million. He wrote or shaped the story for every earlier film in the series.
item.content:encoded:
For the first time this year, Belvedere resident Andrew Stanton can relax after a stretch that left him, in his own words, “super exhausted.”

He’s on the other side of the country, in New York, spending the summer recharging after two big projects overlapped, along with the extensive travel each demanded.

“Doing the global domination tour at 60 is not as easy as it was when you’re 50,” Stanton says.

The global domination, in this case, was directing a film that has grossed more than $900 million at the box office and counting.

Stanton, 60, is best known as an animator, filmmaker and occasional voice actor. He directed “Toy Story 5,” which reached theaters June 19. It’s his first time directing a film in the franchise, though he has written or contributed the story for every prior installment, beginning with the original “Toy Story” in 1995.

Now vice president of creative at Emeryville-based Pixar Animation Studios, Stanton co-directed “A Bug’s Life” and directed “Finding Nemo” and “WALL-E,” both of which won the Academy Award for best animated feature, in 2003 and 2008. He also directed “Finding Dory,” which grossed $1 billion after its 2016 release.
item.dc:creator: Francisco Martinez
item.media:description: Belvedere resident Andrew Stanton’s released two feature-length films in 2026: ‘Toy Story 5’ and ‘In the Blink of an Eye,’ the latter of which he’s seen here directing. ‘In the Blink of an Eye’ follows three stories set in three eras: prehistory, the present and a future in space. (via Andrew Stanton)

item.title: Paradise Cove gets A+ for summer and wet-weather water quality
item.description: Only 78% of Marin beaches earned A's or B's this summer, far below the five-year average of 97%. County officials called the drop unusual and want it investigated.
item.content:encoded:
Paradise Cove has again earned an A-plus grade for water quality from a pollution-tracking watchdog, even as Marin’s countywide grades slipped below their usual marks.

The county’s assessment, released by the Environmental Health Services Division on July 15, draws on the 36th annual Beach Report Card from Heal the Bay, an environmental nonprofit that grades pollution levels at more than 650 beaches from Tijuana to Washington using data collected by local agencies.

Some 78% of Marin beaches received A’s or B’s during the summer dry-weather season, the county said, including Paradise Cove, home to Paradise Beach Park in unincorporated Tiburon. Paradise Cove was one of four Marin beaches to earn an A-plus summer grade, along with Horseshoe Cove in Fort Baker, Dillon Beach and central Muir Beach. It was one of just three — with Horseshoe Cove and Dillon Beach — to earn A-plus marks in both summer and wet weather.

The 78% share fell well short of the five-year average of 97% for beaches earning A’s or B’s, a drop county officials called unusual “since lower rainfall is typically associated with better water quality.” The county said the trend warrants further investigation.
item.dc:creator: Francisco Martinez
item.media:description: Picnickers and pickup soccer players fill the lawn at Paradise Beach Park on July 4, 2024. Paradise Cove again earned an A-plus for water quality in both the summer and wet-weather seasons, one of only three Marin beaches to do so. (Ted McDonnell archive / For The Ark 2024)

item.title: Richardson Bay Sanitary rejects grand jury’s call to consolidate
item.description: District Manager Johnny Tucker says consolidation talk resurfaces every six or eight years. "We don't have time to continually go back and back and back and beat this dead horse."
item.content:encoded:
Richardson Bay Sanitary District officials have rejected every finding and recommendation in a Marin civil grand jury report urging the county’s more than 50 special districts to explore consolidation, with the district’s manager saying the idea has already been studied at length and offers no savings.

The board of directors voted unanimously July 21 to approve the district’s response to the report, “Better Service at Lower Cost — Optimizing Essential Services for the Future of Marin,” released June 11. Named districts are legally required to respond by Sept. 11.

The grand jury found that the fragmented structure of Marin’s special districts creates duplication, uneven fees and service levels, staffing vulnerabilities and weaker long-term resilience across the county.

District officials countered that consolidation had previously been explored and that the report failed to account for districts that have already combined some operations or to recognize the financial challenges a merger would bring.

“By reading this, what I took from it was it was well-written and crafted, it has legs, but if you are a tiny organization that is completely understaffed and doesn’t have good leadership, it has merit,” board President Peter McIntosh said during the meeting. “For our district, I believe it does not have merit.”
item.dc:creator: Francisco Martinez

item.title: Belvedere backs expansion of shared dock on Strip
item.description: The Beach Road applicants dropped plans for wood platforms on the city-owned Strip after residents objected to private building on the public shoreline.
item.content:encoded:
The owners of two adjoining Beach Road homes in Belvedere may enlarge their shared dock and add two boat lifts — but not the structures they had sought on the city-owned Strip.

The Belvedere Planning Commission voted 4-0 July 21 to allow a 270-square-foot expansion of the existing fixed dock at 310 and 312 Beach Road, along with two new boat lifts and a pair of kayak racks on the city-owned water parcel in Belvedere Cove. The homes are owned by Mark Conroe, at 310, and Scott and Nancy Robertson, at 312. Commissioners Don Schinske and Ghazaleh Jamei were absent, and Isolde Wilson served as an alternate.

The dock is subject to a shared lease with the city that runs through 2039. The commission conditioned its approval on reducing the number of walkway lights on the dock, consistent with a staff recommendation to cut the 35 proposed fixtures to no more than 20, and on using the most open of three kayak-rack designs that Conroe presented.

Senior Planner Samie Malakiman said Conroe and the Robertsons scaled back the request in the days before the hearing, dropping wood platforms and a revocable license for the Strip after residents raised concerns about building on the city-owned shoreline.
item.dc:creator: Tyler Callister

item.title: Everyday Encounters: A Belvedere resident reflects on pros, cons of growing up in Marin
item.description: He calls the county a weird dichotomy, a place with a countercultural history and, he says, a lot of Connecticut NIMBYs.
item.content:encoded:
Jonathan Evans says he has an atypical view of Marin. Both of his parents were raised in Stinson Beach, in the area’s bohemian counterculture.

“The culture was very out there,” says the 29-year-old Belvedere resident. “A lot of colorful characters. People that were artists.”

His father drove a dump truck, and his mother was a nursing assistant. Evans, who grew up in Corte Madera, says his family’s background was different from the majority of his peers in the Reed Union School District and at Redwood High School.

“It was weird to go to school with a bunch of kids whose parents worked in private equity,” he says.

After high school, Evans sought something different. He and his now-wife left Marin and lived in cities all over the country, including Santa Rosa; Portland, Oregon; Austin; New York; and finally Atlanta, where Evans earned his bachelor’s degree in computer science from Georgia State University.
item.dc:creator: Tyler Callister
item.media:description: Jonathan Evans of Belvedere, whose parents were raised in Stinson Beach, returned to Marin in February after nearly a decade of moving city to city. (Tyler Callister / The Ark)

item.title: Barbara Paula Mogerman
item.description: Barbara Paula Mogerman has died at age 88.
item.content:encoded:
Barbara was born to Mary and George Troutfelt on January 10, 1938, in San Francisco, California. As a small child, she was enrolled in tap dancing school, where she excelled and found great joy. It wasn’t long until Barbara was dancing in her “Shirley Temple curls” to entertain the American soldiers during World War II.

As a preteen, Barbara’s family relocated from San Francisco to Salt Lake City. During her senior year of high school, Barbara met a young medical student, Stanley Neal Mogerman. As a college freshman at the University of Utah, Barbara was reintroduced to Stan at a Hillel party. He soon became the love of her life. At 18 and 23 years old, Barbara and Stan were married.

Two years into their marriage, the young couple moved to San Francisco where Stan began his medical internship at the newly built Kaiser Foundation Hospital on Geary Boulevard. During Stan’s residency at Kaiser, their eldest daughter, Julie, was born. Three years later, Barbara and Stan purchased their first home, an atrium Eichler in Terra Linda where their other two daughters, Diana and then Laura arrived into the world. In 1972, they moved their young family into their dream home in Tiburon.

Barbara and Stan maintained a deep love during their marriage of 58 years, until Stan’s passing in 2014. They enjoyed a full life of traveling, ballroom dancing and spending time with their children, grandchildren, extended family and friends.

Barbara is survived by her daughters: Julie Goldwyn (David), Diana Maureen (Glenn) and Laura LaBouve (Daniel); five grandchildren: Josh Goldwyn, Bryan Goldwyn, Ashley Maureen, Stephanie LaBouve (Zachary), Eric LaBouve and two great-grandchildren.

In lieu of flowers, please send donations to either By the Bay Health in Larkspur, CA (formerly Hospice by the Bay), or the American Alzheimer’s Association.
item.dc:creator: Reader submitted

item.title: Katherine ‘Katy’ Sarah Nixon Mitchell
item.description: Katy Mitchell, born Katherine Sarah Nixon, passed away peacefully on July 16, 2026, at the age of 106.
item.content:encoded:
Katy Mitchell, born Katherine Sarah Nixon, passed away peacefully on July 16, 2026, at the age of 106. She was born in San Francisco to John Stewart Nixon, of Guayaquil, Ecuador, and Clotilde Cabrales, of Sinaloa, Mexico. Katy grew up in San Pablo, San Jose, and Oakland, and spoke fluent English and Spanish.

She graduated from Fremont High School in 1938 and went on to serve in the U.S. Marine Corps, where she was among the first graduating classes of women Marines in World War II. There she met and married a fellow Marine, Ernie Smith, and gave birth to their daughter, Jeanne. The family later moved to the San Francisco Bay Area, but the marriage did not last.

Katy married Bruce Mitchell in 1949 and made her home in Mill Valley, where their son, Tom, was born. After Tom’s tragic passing in 1968, Katy went back to working full-time as a designer and draftsperson of kitchens and homes. In her free time, she and her family and friends built a second home in the Gold Rush town of La Porte, California.

In 1986, Katy moved to Tiburon, where she lived independently, drove her own car, played golf, and gardened. Above all, she cherished time spent with her grandchildren and great-grandchildren.

Katy is survived by her daughter, Jeanne; her son-in-law, Don; her grandchildren Danielle, Paul, and Natalie, and their spouses; and six great-grandchildren, Graham, Whitaker, Olivia, Teddy, Christian, and Cameron, along with other loving family in the United States and El Salvador.

The family is deeply grateful to the caregivers at AlmaVia of San Rafael and By the Bay Health, formerly Hospice by the Bay. In lieu of flowers, donations may be made to Guide Dogs for the Blind.

item.title: Tradition comes to life at Tiburon Jewish Festival
item.description: Chabad of Tiburon held its fourth annual Tiburon Jewish Festival on July 26 at Zelinsky Park.
item.content:encoded: Saul Goodman’s Klezmer Band, which modernizes Eastern European Jewish folk music, performs at Chabad of Tiburon’s fourth annual Tiburon Jewish Festival on July 26 at Zelinsky Park. At left, Rabbi Levi Potash, a scribe from Redwood City, letters visitors’ names in Hebrew for key chains at the festival, which also offered a challah-making workshop, a Yad Vashem exhibit, kosher food and an ‘Ask the Rabbi’ booth. (Leo Leung / For The Ark)
